tagline: Isan's newest Mekong town — Phu Tok's wooden stairways, the Three Whale Rocks, and rubber plantations as far as you can see
introHtml: Bueng Kan is Thailand's most recently created province, carved out of Nong Khai. It's a quiet town on the Mekong that more people are starting to swing by, drawn by its oddly shaped rock hills. The first thing most people picture is Phu Tok, where wooden stairs and walkways spiral around the cliff all the way to the summit, and the Three Whale Rocks on Phu Sing — huge boulders shaped like a family of whales lying side by side, facing out over the forest. The countryside around the province is green rubber plantations stretching to the horizon, broken up by rice fields. In town there's a riverside road where you can sit in the evening breeze and look across to Laos. Bueng Kan suits anyone who wants to explore the upper Isan in a slow, nature-minded way, driving past quiet scenery without the crowds.
bestTime: November–February, cool weather that makes walking Phu Tok and climbing the Three Whale Rocks comfortable, with clear skies and long views. The rainy season turns the rubber plantations and waterfalls lush green, but the trails up the hills can get slippery.

highlights.name: Phu Tok
highlights.blurb: A rock hill wrapped in wooden stairs and walkways that spiral up the cliff face level by level to the summit. It's a meditation site belonging to Wat Chetiyakhiri Wihan, and the climb rewards you with views over forest and open plains — the number-one image people have of Bueng Kan.

highlights.name: Three Whale Rocks
highlights.blurb: A cluster of huge boulders on Phu Sing shaped like a whale family — parent and calves — lying in a row. Stand on the rock and you look out over forest and the distant Mekong; it's a popular spot to catch the sunrise.

highlights.name: Mekong Riverside Road
highlights.blurb: The walkway and road along the river in central Bueng Kan where people come out to sit in the breeze, cycle, and stroll in the evening, looking across to the Laos side. There are markets and riverside restaurants here.

highlights.name: Rubber Plantations
highlights.blurb: Bueng Kan is Isan's rubber-tapping province, and the roadsides are lined with rows of green rubber trees as far as you can see. Driving through feels different from the rest of the region.

highlights.name: Bueng Khong Long
highlights.blurb: A large freshwater lake and non-hunting area that's home to waterbirds and migratory birds in the cool season. There are viewpoints and lakeside paths where you can sit quietly in the breeze.

highlights.name: Waterfalls and Hills of Phu Wua Forest
highlights.blurb: The Phu Wua Wildlife Sanctuary has several waterfalls, including Jet Si (Seven-Colour) Falls and Tham Phra Falls. In the rainy season the water tumbles hard in tiers, shaded by forest — the province's main nature draw.

foodScene.name: Isan Food
foodScene.note: Som tam, laap, koi, grilled chicken, and bold bamboo-shoot soup are the everyday meals in Bueng Kan, just like across the region. You'll find them in every corner of town from morning to night.

foodScene.name: Mekong River Fish
foodScene.note: Riverside restaurants cook up freshwater fish — grilled, in tom yum, as laap pla, and pla khang catfish. Eat in the cool breeze with a view across to Laos.

foodScene.name: Vietnamese Food
foodScene.note: Naem nueang, mu yo, and khao piak sen turn up at shops around town, thanks to the Thai-Vietnamese community roots along the Mekong — much like the other river towns.

foodScene.name: Mu Krata and Grilled Meats
foodScene.note: Mu krata (Thai BBQ hot pot) joints are scattered all over town and make for a dinner that groups gather around, especially along the main roads and near the river.

foodScene.name: Kuai Chap Yuan
foodScene.note: Soft Vietnamese-style rice noodles in a clear broth dusted with pepper — a popular breakfast influenced by the Vietnamese community along the river. Look for it at the morning markets.

foodScene.name: Cafes and Coffee in Town
foodScene.note: Lately a number of new cafes have opened both in town and along the river, some set in the middle of rubber plantations. A good place to sip coffee and rest before heading up Phu Tok or the Three Whale Rocks.

foodScene.name: Street Food and Evening Markets
foodScene.note: The town and riverside markets have grilled and fried snacks and local sweets to graze on after dark, all at friendly prices.

foodScene.name: Souvenirs from Laos
foodScene.note: Mu yo, naem, dried goods, and products from the Laos side are easy to find at the riverside markets — easy things to pick up and take home.

attractions.name: Phu Tok and Wat Chetiyakhiri Wihan
attractions.blurb: A rock hill with wooden walkways and stairs that spiral around the cliff face up to the summit. It's a meditation site and a viewpoint over forest and open plains — the signature image of Bueng Kan.

attractions.name: Three Whale Rocks, Phu Sing
attractions.blurb: A group of huge boulders shaped like a whale family lying in a row on Phu Sing. Stand here for views of forest and the distant Mekong; it's a popular sunrise spot, reached by guided pickup truck.

attractions.name: Mekong Riverside Road in Town
attractions.blurb: The walkway and road along the river in town where people come out to sit in the breeze, cycle, and stroll in the evening, looking across to Laos. There are restaurants and riverside markets.

attractions.name: Bueng Khong Long
attractions.blurb: A large freshwater lake and non-hunting area, a place to watch waterbirds and migratory birds in the cool season. There are viewpoints and lakeside paths where you can sit quietly in the breeze.

attractions.name: Jet Si Waterfall
attractions.blurb: A waterfall in the Phu Wua forest where the water runs across a wide cliff and catches the light in several colours. It runs strong in the rainy season, shaded by forest — good for a swim and a break in nature.

attractions.name: Tham Phra Waterfall, Phu Wua
attractions.blurb: A large waterfall in the Phu Wua Wildlife Sanctuary that takes a fair bit of hiking to reach, with water dropping into a wide pool in the middle of the forest — a trek for nature lovers.

attractions.name: Wat Ahong Silawat
attractions.blurb: A riverside temple at the Ahong rapids whirlpool, believed to be the deepest point of the Mekong. There are shrines and naga figures to pay respects to, with a fine view of the rock rapids midstream.

attractions.name: Phu Langka
attractions.blurb: Forest and hills in the north of the province with multi-tier waterfalls and a sea-of-mist viewpoint in the cool season — good for hikers and for camping to catch the morning view.
